questions.explanation: Conversion efficiency only compares an input with an output of equal quality, and for a resistance element every watt does become heat, so the honest figure really is 100 percent. What that figure hides is the quality of that heat: a litre of air warmed to 20 degrees has almost no capacity to do work once it is sitting at room temperature, while the same litre warmed to 70 degrees is worth something. A heat pump earns its advantage by lifting the temperature of the heat it delivers while paying only for the lifting work, so it can put three or four units of useful room heat into the space for each unit of electricity it buys. The tempting belief is that a higher percentage must mean a better machine, which is why the 100 percent heater and the 90 percent boiler are not being compared on the same question at all.

questions.explanation: A heat pump is a refrigerator run in reverse, so the balance that governs a refrigerator applies unchanged: heat delivered to the warm space equals heat taken from the cold space plus the work the compressor is given. With 1 kW of work and a coefficient of performance of 3, the delivered heat is 3 kW, and the remaining 2 kW was drawn from the outdoor air. That extra term is also why an air source unit keeps working on a freezing day, since the air still holds heat at minus 10 degrees and the machine only has to lift it. The tempting belief is that the work is the only energy in the system, and that is exactly the assumption behind a 100 percent figure. A machine that delivered heat with no work at all would be a second-kind perpetual motion machine, which the second law forbids.

questions.explanation: Work from a heat engine is produced by heat flowing downhill in temperature, and the amount that can be squeezed out depends on how far it falls. For a source at 500 K and a sink at 300 K the ceiling is 1 minus 300 over 500, which is 0.40, and even a frictionless engine operating infinitely slowly cannot beat it. The rejected heat is not waste from a badly made machine; it is the price of the temperature difference, and shrinking the difference between source and sink shrinks the ceiling towards zero. The tempting belief is that every shortfall is an engineering loss, which is why a modern plant's 60 percent is often read as a failure of design. What the law says is that 40 percent is the best this pair of temperatures allows, no matter how good the engineering becomes.

questions.explanation: Total fuel utilisation is the share of the fuel energy that leaves the plant as something someone will pay for, and both the electricity and the steam qualify once the steam is actually delivered to the hospital. Adding 35 and 45 percent gives 80 percent, with the remaining 20 percent leaving in the flue and around the equipment. The tempting belief is that a power station has one useful output, which is why district heat and factory steam are often ignored in the accounts. questions.explanation: Power in a line is voltage times current, so for a fixed delivered power the current falls in direct proportion to the voltage, and the resistive loss in the conductor is current squared times resistance. Raising the line voltage from 33 kV to 230 kV therefore cuts the current by a factor of seven and cuts the resistive loss by a factor of forty-nine, which is why transmission voltage is stepped up wherever the distance makes the conductor expensive. The tempting belief is that the same current flows and only the losses differ, which is the assumption that makes high-voltage transmission look pointless. Voltage and current trade against each other at fixed power, and the conductor is paid for by the current squared.

questions.explanation: A wind turbine is deliberately limited at the top of its range, because the loads that build up in a 3 MW rotor once the wind exceeds the rated speed rise faster than the power does, and survival matters more than output. The rotor does store kinetic energy, but it spins that energy out through the generator within seconds and cannot be banked for later. The tempting belief is that a stopped turbine is a failed turbine, and this is the single most common misreading of a windy night, when most of the fleet is parked precisely because the wind is strong.

questions.explanation: A stack test measures carbon dioxide leaving the boiler, so it captures the chemistry of combustion and nothing that happens in a coal mine, an oil field or a gas well. questions.explanation: The permit defines two quantities and the definition of the second tells the reader which is which: withdrawal is everything drawn from the river, and consumption is the difference between that and what comes back, which is the part lost to evaporation and to the product. A plant that withdraws 900 000 and consumes 120 000 therefore returns 780 000 m3 a day, and its efficiency of heat use and of water use are different numbers. The tempting belief is that two numbers in one permit are the same number written twice, which would let a planner size against 900 000 and believe the water impact was 900 000. The measurable consequence is in the returned flow, since a hotter return is a temperature and a dissolved oxygen problem even when the consumptive loss is small.
questions.hint: Use the definition in the permit: consumption is the withdrawal that does not come back.

options.text: The two limits are the same bound restated, so either may be used for planning

options.misconception: reverses which of the two terms is the intake and which is the loss

questions.explanation: A stated scope defines exactly which question was answered, and this report answers the question of what leaves the stack when the plant burns fuel. That is a real and useful number, and it is the right number for comparing two plants burning different fuels at the same gate. It cannot support a claim about the full chain, because extraction, refining, transport and end of life have been left out, and leaving a stage out of a boundary does not reduce its contribution to the result, it only stops counting it. The tempting belief is that an unquantified stage is a negligible stage, and in a fuel cycle the upstream terms are frequently the same order as the stack term. Naming a boundary is a strength, and it is the moment a reader decides whether the question being answered is the question being asked.
questions.hint: Ask which stages the report answers for, and which it has set aside.
questions.learningObjective: identify the claim a scoped report can license

questions.explanation: The capacity charge is set by the highest 15 minute demand, so a 6 kW peak gives 6 times 14 which is 84, and it is waived only in a month with less than 500 kWh of use, so 600 kWh of use leaves the waiver out of play. The decisive point is that the peak and the energy are independent quantities: a household that heats a kettle and nothing else for an hour has high energy and no meaningful demand, while one that runs a 6 kW load for two minutes has a high peak and almost no energy. The tempting belief is that the waiver makes the capacity charge a function of consumption, and it is not, because the threshold is a gate rather than a scale. For a large user this is why load shifting has value even when no energy is saved.
questions.hint: Identify which of the two quantities sets the capacity charge, and what the waiver tests.

questions.explanation: The diagram shows one fuel stream branching into a grid output, a useful heat output and a loss, and the three arrows move together when the fuel flow changes. With a second heat customer, the 45 percent stream can be sold instead of being dumped, so the flue share of 20 percent is a candidate for reduction rather than a fixed tax, and the whole point of combined heat and power is that the arrow pointing at the stack becomes an arrow pointing at a building. The tempting belief is that flue losses are a constant percentage locked to the plant, and the second temptation is that a second customer takes heat away from the first, when in practice an additional load is usually met from capacity that was previously dumped. What cannot grow is the electricity share unless a turbine is added, because it is the smallest and least flexible of the three.

questions.explanation: Resistive loss in a conductor is current squared times resistance, and for a fixed delivered power the current is set by the voltage, so the highest-voltage stage carries the least current and therefore loses the least per unit of energy sent. Raising transmission voltage, or sending more of the power at a higher voltage, attacks the same kilowatt-hour of loss more cheaply than rebuilding the last mile, where the current is largest. There is a second and more important point about the transformer: a distribution transformer has a no-load loss that it burns continuously whether the customer is using anything or not, which is a different mechanism from the I squared R term and responds to a different intervention. The tempting belief is that the loss nearest the customer is the largest, which confuses proximity with current.
questions.hint: Compare the current at each stage for the same delivered power.

options.misconception: mislabels a billing error as a physical loss that can be engineered away
options.text: At the consumer meter, because a meter that overstates use saves the most energy

options.misconception: assumes a fixed ranking of losses between components

questions.explanation: The stages are in series, so their efficiencies multiply: 0.80 times 0.96 times 0.90 is 0.691, so the chain delivers about 69 percent of incident light before the fault, and derating the inverter to 0.90 gives 0.80 times 0.90 times 0.90, which is 0.648 or about 65 percent. The ratio of the two results, 0.90 over 0.96, is the factor by which one derated stage changes the chain, so the fall of about 4 percentage points is consistent with a 6 percent loss in one stage rather than a loss across the system. The tempting belief is that the stages can be added, subtracted or weighted equally, and in a series path a weak stage caps the whole chain no matter how good the others are. A parallel or standby path is the only structure in which a single derating does not propagate.
questions.hint: Multiply the three stage efficiencies in the order shown in the path.

options.text: About 96 percent, because the inverter is the only stage that has changed
